original_question: How can the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks be related to other theories of wild ramification?
target_in_paper: Section 11, Problem 11.1 ("Relation to other theories on wild ramification"): "Relate the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks with other theories on wild ramification."
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's official formulation. It correctly identifies the exact two subjects named in Problem 11.1—the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks—and it asks for their relation to other theories of/on wild ramification, which is precisely the direction of Section 11.
missing_details: The paper's standing convention is that the base field k is algebraically closed unless otherwise specified.
The relevant setting for the wild McKay correspondence in Section 2.3 is a faithful linear action of a finite group G on an affine space V = A^d_k, usually assumed to have no pseudo-reflections.
The word "wild" is implicit in your draft but, in the paper, it means char(k) = p > 0 and p divides |G| (or the orders of stabilizers/isotropy groups).
The formal content of the wild McKay correspondence is not stated in your draft: the paper writes it as the stringy-motive identity M_st(X) = integral over Delta_G of L^(-w) d tau for X = V/G.
The paper explicitly rephrases the same identity as M_st(X) = M_st([V/G]); this quotient-stack formulation is part of the intended meaning of the problem.

The symbols M_st, L, Delta_G, w, and d tau are all implicit in the paper's formulation of the surrounding theory and are absent from the draft; here M_st is the stringy motive, L the Lefschetz motive, Delta_G the moduli space of G-torsors over Spec k((t)), w the weight function, and d tau the motivic measure.
Section 11 frames the question as part of a higher-dimensional theory of wild ramification via a restriction-to-curves viewpoint; your draft does not include that perspective.
The nearby context gives a concrete comparison direction—non-liftability of arcs along wildly ramified finite covers—but your draft does not mention this example.
A Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich-type formula is separated off as Problem 11.2, so a paper-faithful rewrite should not merge that neighboring problem into Problem 11.1.
There are no paper-specific conditions here involving homogeneity, polynomial degree, nilpotency, or phrases such as "for all sufficiently large m"; those notions are not part of this problem.
refined_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic p > 0, and let a finite group G act faithfully and linearly on V = A^d_k without pseudo-reflections, with p dividing |G|; write X = V/G. In the wild McKay framework, the stringy motive of X is given by the motivic integral M_st(X) = integral over Delta_G of L^(-w) d tau, where Delta_G is the moduli space of G-torsors over the punctured formal disk Spec k((t)), w: Delta_G -> Q is the weight function, L is the Lefschetz motive, and d tau is the motivic measure; equivalently, M_st(X) = M_st([V/G]). Can one formulate and prove precise comparison results relating this wild McKay/motivic-integration formalism for [V/G]—and, more generally, motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks—to other existing theories on wild ramification in higher dimensions, especially those arising from the restriction-to-curves viewpoint and from phenomena such as non-liftability of arcs along wildly ramified finite covers?
equivalent_formulation: In the same setting, relate the quotient-stack form of the wild McKay correspondence, M_st(X) = M_st([V/G]), together with motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks, to other theories on wild ramification. This is equivalent here because Section 2.3 explicitly rephrases the integral identity M_st(X) = integral over Delta_G of L^(-w) d tau as M_st(X) = M_st([V/G]).
justification: The draft is targeting Section 11, Problem 11.1 almost verbatim. The introduction says that Section 11 is devoted to problems on the relation of the wild McKay correspondence and other theories in terms of wild ramification. Section 11 then states Problem 11.1 exactly in the language echoed by your draft. To make the question stand alone while staying paper-faithful, one must import the paper's standard conventions and the formal meaning of "wild McKay correspondence" from Sections 2.1 and 2.3: wildness means positive characteristic with group order divisible by the characteristic, and the correspondence is expressed by the stringy-motive identity for X = V/G, or equivalently by the quotient-stack equality M_st(X) = M_st([V/G]). The nearby discussion in Section 11 further clarifies the intended comparison: the theory is viewed as a higher-dimensional approach to wild ramification via restriction to curves, with non-liftability of arcs along wildly ramified finite covers given as the concrete motivating example. Problem 11.2 separately isolates the Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich direction, so it should not be folded into the refined version of Problem 11.1.
